summary.text: A Cepheid variable is a star that pulsates, changing in both diameter and temperature, so its brightness varies with a well-defined stable period.
Its pulsation period is directly related to its luminosity, so timing the pulses tells astronomers how luminous the star truly is.
Comparing that luminosity with the star's observed brightness gives its distance, which makes Cepheids benchmarks for galactic and extragalactic distances.

facts.label: Link discovered
facts.value: By Henrietta Swan Leavitt in 1908, using Magellanic Cloud stars

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: The star Delta Cephei, in the constellation Cepheus

facts.label: Hubble in 1924
facts.value: Cepheids showed Andromeda lies outside the Milky Way

items.prompt: How do astronomers use a Cepheid to find how far away it is?

options.label: Its pulse timing reveals its true brightness, which is compared with how bright it looks
Its colour reveals its true size, and size sets the distance
Its pulse timing shows how fast it is moving away
Its pulse size shows how long its light took to arrive

items.explain: The period gives the true luminosity, and comparing that with the observed brightness gives the distance.

items.prompt: What best explains why a Cepheid's outer layer cycles between squeezing and swelling?

options.label: A companion star repeatedly pulls on it
Helium alternates between a heat-trapping form and a transparent form
Fusion in its core switches on and off each cycle
It spins so fast that its shape wobbles

items.explain: Compression heats helium until it is doubly ionized and more opaque; it then absorbs heat, expands, cools, becomes singly ionized and transparent, and collapses again.

items.prompt: Edwin Hubble found Cepheids in the Andromeda Nebula and worked out how far away they were. What did this show?

options.label: Andromeda is a gas cloud inside the Milky Way
The Milky Way is the only galaxy that exists
Cepheids only ever occur inside nebulae
Andromeda lies outside the Milky Way, so it is not the whole Universe

items.explain: He showed the variables were not members of the Milky Way, settling the Great Debate over whether it was the entire Universe.

items.prompt: Astronomers once treated all Cepheids as one family and their distances came out wrong. What did Baade's discovery reveal?

options.label: Two kinds exist, with different period-luminosity relationships
All Cepheids share one age but sit at different distances
Cepheids brighten by two different pulsation mechanisms
Only one of the two kinds actually pulsates

items.explain: Baade recognized classical and type II Cepheids, which follow different period-luminosity relationships; dividing them resolved problems with the distance scale.

items.prompt: Early on, a Cepheid's velocity was seen to vary with the same period as its brightness, and a hidden companion was suspected. Was that right?

options.label: Yes, every Cepheid was later found to have a companion
Yes, the companion explains the period-luminosity link
No, the star itself changes each cycle and the idea was dropped
No, the velocity changes were shown to be instrument errors

items.explain: Shapley demonstrated the binary idea should be abandoned and found that Cepheids change their spectral types over a cycle.

items.prompt: Besides measuring distances to other galaxies, what have Cepheids helped astronomers learn about our own?

options.label: The Sun's exact age and how many planets circle it
The Sun's height above the galactic plane and local spiral shape
Where the exact center of the whole Universe lies
The temperature at the very core of the Milky Way

items.explain: Classical Cepheids have been used to clarify characteristics of the Milky Way, such as the Sun's height above the galactic plane and the local spiral structure.
